analysis.one_liner: Immediately ends the federal tax credit paid to companies for blending ethanol into gasoline.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to repeal the ethanol tax credit drew 19 Senate cosponsors but died in the Senate Finance Committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law gave fuel blenders a tax credit for every gallon of ethanol they mixed into gasoline, a subsidy costing taxpayers roughly $6 billion a year that was scheduled to lapse at the end of 2011. This bill would have ended it immediately, stopping the payments right away instead of letting them run out on the scheduled date. The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, a vote, or any further action before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who would stop paying roughly $6 billion a year in ethanol blending credits, and drivers in markets where the subsidy inflates the price of ethanol-blended fuel. Groups across the political spectrum, from fiscal conservatives to environmental and anti-hunger organizations, supported ending the subsidy.

how_it_helps.text: The bill immediately repeals the volumetric ethanol excise tax credit and the parallel income tax credit for alcohol fuel mixtures, ending payments that were otherwise scheduled to continue through December 31, 2011.

The credits are paid to companies that blend ethanol into motor fuel, so repeal stops federal reimbursements of roughly $6 billion a year and removes a subsidy that raises the price of ethanol relative to gasoline.
The bill also cleans up the 'deadwood' code provisions that would become moot once the credits end, making the repeal effective immediately upon enactment.

analysis.who_pays: The ethanol industry and its blenders, mostly large oil refiners that collect the credit, plus corn growers who sell to ethanol plants. Rural communities built around ethanol production would face lower demand and thinner margins.

drawbacks.text: Ending the subsidy immediately, rather than on the scheduled expiration date, would cut roughly $6 billion a year in revenue that ethanol producers and blenders had counted on, pressuring plant margins and the rural jobs and corn demand that depend on them.

The blending credit lowers the effective price of ethanol in gasoline, so immediate repeal would modestly raise fuel costs at the margin in the short run until ethanol competed on price without the credit.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The subsidy primarily reimbursed blenders for doing something federal law already required them to do under the renewable fuel standard, so most economists regarded the credit as a pure transfer that mainly benefited blenders and corn growers rather than producing new ethanol. Repealing it saved taxpayer money at a modest cost to a mature industry. The bill's main weakness was timing: the credit was already set to expire on December 31, 2011, so the practical savings were limited to the months between enactment and that date. In the event, the credit lapsed on schedule anyway, which makes the bill's fate largely about whether Congress could act on a subsidy years earlier than the expiration date it had already set.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Senator Tom Coburn introduced the bill on March 9, 2011 together with Senator Benjamin Cardin, a Democrat, and it gathered 19 cosponsors split 14 Republicans and 5 Democrats.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance the day it was introduced, and the action history shows no further steps: no hearing, no markups, no vote.
The ethanol tax credit the bill targeted was scheduled to expire on December 31, 2011 under existing law.
The credit was allowed to lapse at the end of 2011 without renewal, but through separate legislative action, not through this bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The ethanol industry and its blenders came out ahead in the short run: the bill's death meant the blending credit kept flowing through its full scheduled life into the end of 2011, and Congress never had to take the politically difficult vote on ending it. Taxpayers eventually got most of the savings anyway only because the credit's expiration date arrived, not because this bill moved.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, bringing total sponsorship to 19 senators (14 Republicans, 5 Democrats).

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction (Chair: Sen. Max Baucus, D-MT)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral and took no further action on the bill for the rest of the Congress; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever scheduled.

against.name: Ethanol industry and corn grower groups
against.role: Recipients and defenders of the blending credit
against.what_they_did: Opposed immediate repeal of the blending credit, defending a subsidy worth roughly $6 billion a year to the industry.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was bipartisan, with 19 Senate cosponsors split 14 Republicans and 5 Democrats; its death in committee reflected the Senate's failure to act rather than opposition on the floor.

industries.note: The blending credit reimbursed companies for each gallon of ethanol mixed into gasoline, about $6 billion a year, and repeal ended it immediately. Blenders, largely large oil refiners, collected the payments, so the industry's interest in keeping the subsidy ran directly against taxpayers' interest in ending it.

Roughly a third of the U.S. corn crop goes to ethanol plants, and the blending credit supports demand and prices for corn. Farmers did not receive the credit directly but benefited from the demand it sustained.
Ending the credit stops roughly $6 billion a year in federal payments. Because the credit mainly reimbursed blenders for a mandated practice, the savings came at little cost to fuel supply.
